Artificial intelligence is currently a tailwind, not a threat, on the company's own measured data. Management moved from a defensive answer in mid-2025 ("We don't see it as a negative") to an affirmative, evidenced one by the first quarter of 2026: "we see a positive impact from AI tools, which make content and website creation faster and easier." Query volume rose from over 460 billion per day (second quarter of 2025) to 600 billion (first quarter of 2026), roughly 30% in nine months - reliance on the resolution layer is rising as AI use rises.

There are two free options in the price. First, new services: management previewed in the fourth quarter of 2025 that it has "strong candidates for new services that can help reduce known and unknown vulnerabilities," firmed in the first quarter of 2026 into a blog series on "high assurance infrastructure." This would be the first business expansion after years of divestitures and is in no model. Second, .web - a top-level domain the company won at auction in 2016 and intends to operate, still tied up in arbitration.

Capital returns are heavy and consistent: $1.1B returned in 2025 and $1.13B in the twelve months to the first quarter of 2026 - over 100% of free cash flow - through buybacks (with $863M of authorization remaining) and a dividend initiated in 2025 at $0.77 and raised 5.2% to $0.81. The buyback shrinks the share count roughly 3.5% a year, which is why earnings per share compound near 10% on 6.5% revenue growth. Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway owns close to 10% of the company - a permanent, non-forced holder.

The conditions this case depends on: the domain base keeps growing 3-4% a year; registrars absorb or pass through the November price increase without a visible hit to renewals; the AI tailwind on registrations persists rather than inverting; and the market is willing to pay a quasi-monopoly multiple for a 6-7% grower.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that VeriSign is a bad business. It is that you are being asked to pay a full price for a business whose good news has already been announced, whose long-term demand question is genuinely unresolved, and whose reported numbers hide a discount only management can see.

Start with price. At $275.22 the shares trade at roughly 30 times trailing earnings of $9.05 and about 24 times enterprise value to free cash flow - 12% below the 52-week high of $312.48 and 32% above the low, 5% above the 200-day average, 60% up the 52-week range. Nothing here is washed out. The scan's own model reads a negative 26% margin of safety against a $200.63 fair value. The market has already watched this recovery for five straight quarters and priced it: the shares fell about 6.5% on 2026-04-24, the day after a strong first-quarter report that contained the price-increase announcement. When a stock falls on good news that management pre-announced three months earlier, the re-rate is spent.

The growth is thinner than the narrative. Revenue compounds at 5.2% over three years and grew 6.4% in 2025; earnings per share grow about 10%. The wedge is a buyback funded increasingly by the balance sheet. Net debt is $1.24B as of 2026-03-31 (borrowings $1.79B plus $6M of capitalized leases, less $556M of cash; roughly $1.23B excluding leases) and cash has drifted down across five quarters - $649M, $594M, $618M, $581M, $556M - while the company returns more than 100% of free cash flow. Roughly a third of the earnings growth is financial engineering with a finite runway. Book equity is negative, a legacy of buying back stock above book value.

Every line of the 2026 guide points the wrong way beneath a rising top line. Capital expenditure roughly doubles to $55-65M from $25-35M, and management's stated reason is uncomfortable: hardware costs are "facing significantly higher costs largely attributable to intense AI industry-driven demand and supply constraints." VeriSign is a buyer of the same equipment the AI build-out is bidding up. Operating margin is guided back down toward "our long-term trend" from the 2025 level; the tax rate steps up to 22-25% on foreign taxes; interest expense rises to $57-67M. The screener reads margins 1.08 standard deviations above their historical peak - management is saying the same thing in words.

The least transparent part of the story is the one driving the recovery. In the third quarter of 2025 the finance chief conceded the marketing programs "are accounted for as a reduction in revenue." The discount funding the domain-base recovery is netted against the top line and never disclosed as a number. Reported 6.4% revenue growth is after an unquantified concession, and when Citi pressed directly on whether there had been "a lot of discounting within that," the answer was a non-answer about "higher quality and higher renewing names." Only management knows the gross figure, and the recovery's durability rests on it.

The price increase is not free, and management will not say it is. Asked directly about elasticity after November 1, the finance chief said it is "very dependent on what our retail registrars do pricing-wise. If they do take price increases, that could have an effect on either new registrations or renewals. And we've seen a little bit of that in the past." Layer on a self-inflicted headwind the company has now flagged twice: 2026 carries a heavier mix of first-time renewals, which mathematically drags the blended renewal rate lower even if underlying behaviour is unchanged. The favourable renewal-rate optics of 2025 partially reverse in 2026 by arithmetic.

The terminal question is unanswered. If users ask an assistant instead of typing an address, and if autonomous agents transact through machine identifiers rather than memorable human-readable names, demand for a .com decays and the long tail of the base shrinks. Management addresses the near-term volume tailwind with data and dodges the agentic question with assertion ("we believe demand for persistent, resolvable identities and endpoints will continue"). And the chief executive has already conceded that one slice of the base - domains parked for advertising revenue - has been "on a downhill slide for 15 years" since Google's Panda update, while refusing to size it: "I don't have a segment breakout in detail. We do some analysis, but we don't disclose that."

The insiders vote against the story. Open-market activity is 5 buys totalling 54 shares against 51 sells totalling 37,088 shares. The people who know the discount, the elasticity and the parked-domain exposure are net sellers by roughly 690-to-1 by volume.

Structurally, the moat is a contract, and contracts expire. The .com registry agreement runs to November 2030; the price cap is set by the US Department of Commerce, not by the market; the company is "prohibited from selling .com registrations to retail buyers" and may sell only to accredited registrars "at a capped regulated price." Meanwhile the channel it must sell through is consolidating, and its largest customer, GoDaddy, is price-unrestricted. The risk here was never a competitor; it is a renewal negotiation, a political mood, or a regulator that decides a legal monopoly on the internet's address book should not compound its price 7% a year.

What would confirm the bear: renewal rates rolling over after 2026-11-01; the domain-base guide being cut rather than raised at the 2026-07-23 report; new registrations falling back below 10 million a quarter; or any softening in the political posture toward the price escalator.
consensus_delta:
The honest answer is the uncomfortable one for a committee that gets paid to disagree: on VeriSign, we do not disagree with the market. Our parts-based fair value of about $272, our discounted cash flow at about $268, and the live price of $275.22 sit within 2% of each other. Where we disagree is with the two loudest published opinions, which sit on either side of us and are both wrong.

First, the sell-side anchor is not a street view at all - it is one analyst. The consensus, median, high and low price targets are all $355.00, which is arithmetic proof that a single estimate is carrying the entire number: Robert W. Baird, dated 2026-04-24, when the stock was $276.95, and now 84 days old. Exactly one price target printed in the last quarter and two in the last year. That target implies about 31% upside, which requires roughly 29-30x enterprise value to free cash flow - the full toll-franchise cohort multiple applied to a business growing 6-7% against a cohort growing high-single to low-teens, with a price cap set by the Department of Commerce and a contract expiring in November 2030. It is a fair-weather multiple for a franchise that is legally leased rather than owned. The system's own screener repeats the +31% upside as though it were a street-wide view; it is one desk's opinion, and treating it as consensus would be the error.

Second, the published bear anchor is equally wrong in the other direction. A 2026-07-15 note puts intrinsic value at $217 and calls the stock 20% overpriced, preferring entry below $200. That requires paying roughly 20x free cash flow for a business with 88.2% gross margins, a 64.5% free-cash-flow margin, a legally exclusive franchise, a contractual right to raise prices about 7% a year in each of four straight years, and a domain base at a record 176.1 million and accelerating. That price gets paid in a panic, not in a market that is up 9.3% for the year with volatility at 16.6.

The real expectations question is where the street's genuine blind spot lives, and it is not the price increase - it is the discount funding the volume recovery. In the third quarter of 2025 the finance chief conceded that the marketing programs "are accounted for as a reduction in revenue." That means reported revenue growth of 6.4% is net of an undisclosed concession to registrars, and when Citi pressed directly on whether there had been "a lot of discounting within that," management answered about "higher quality and higher renewing names" instead. Every model on the street extrapolates a domain-base recovery whose cost no outside party can measure. That is a real information asymmetry - but it cuts against a long position, not for one, and it is not resolvable from the outside. Insiders, who can see it, have bought 54 shares and sold 37,088 on the open market.

The second blind spot is one management disclosed twice and the market has largely filed away: 2026 carries a heavier mix of first-time renewals, which mathematically drags the blended renewal rate lower even if underlying behaviour is unchanged. The flattering renewal optics of 2025 partially reverse by arithmetic in 2026. Anyone modelling 76.3% forward is modelling a number the company has already told them will fade.

What the market is right about, and what a deep-value screen mislabels: this is not a deep-value name. It is a wide-moat compounder at roughly 30x trailing earnings, 12% off its 52-week high, 32% above its low, 5% above its 200-day average, 60% up the 52-week range. There is no crowd looking the wrong way here. The screener's own deep-value framing - is the street pricing terminal decline into a company with stable earnings power? - answers itself: the street is pricing durable growth into a company with durable growth, and charging a fair price for it.
forcing_function:
There isn't one - and after checking each candidate against a calendar, that is the finding rather than an absence of research.

The strongest candidate has already fired. The .com price increase to $10.97 takes effect on 2026-11-01, a hard and contractually binding date. But the notice was given on 2026-04-23, the mechanism was pre-announced on the 2026-02-05 call, the amount is capped by contract at about 7%, and the shares fell about 6.5% the day the news landed. Every model on the street already has the November revenue in it. A dated cash event that everyone can compute is not a forcing function; it is an accounting entry with a calendar.

Second-quarter results land on 2026-07-23, six days from now - dated and confirmed. But it forces nothing. A management team that has raised guidance at five consecutive calls has made its own beat the consensus. The one genuinely non-consensus outcome would be a *cut* to the domain-base guide, which would break the thesis rather than confirm it - an asymmetry pointing the wrong way for a buyer.

The next real pricing decision is roughly nine months out. Management confirmed the mechanic: six months' notice is required, so the next increase, if taken, would be announced around April 2027 for a November 2027 effective date. That is outside any reasonable window and, once again, fully predictable in size.

The .web arbitration could in principle deliver a windfall - a new top-level domain to operate at near-zero incremental infrastructure cost. It is a soft, non-binding, third-party matter and the definition of a serially-extended catalyst: a 2016 auction, one completed arbitration cycle, a second still running, a final hearing scheduled for mid-November 2025 with no outcome reported as of today, eight months later. Management's own updates decayed from substantive (first and second quarters of 2025) to "nothing substantive that's new" (third quarter of 2025) to silence. They have stopped underwriting it, and so should we.

The new high-assurance security services are the most interesting thing in the file and the least investable today. Previewed in the fourth quarter of 2025 as "strong candidates for new services," firmed in the first quarter of 2026 into a promised blog series. No product, no price, no revenue, no date. It is a reason to keep reading the calls, not a reason to buy the stock.

ICANN's new top-level-domain round opened in April 2026 with applications closing in August 2026 and deployment unlikely before 2027. Management has said only that it is "studying it" with "nothing to report yet" - and, notably, that all applications become public shortly after the round opens. That is a genuine dated information event in August, but VeriSign has given no indication it will be a material applicant, and a new top-level domain would be immaterial against .com for years.

There is no activist, no strategic process, no governance reset, no sum-of-the-parts discount to unlock, and no conceivable premium scenario: a $25B company holding a US-government-conditioned monopoly on the internet's address book is not acquirable, and its parts sum to approximately its whole. On the Third Point test - catalyst density, parts discount, activism potential, asymmetric risk and reward - VeriSign scores near zero on all four. It is an exceptionally well-run business with nothing for an event-driven committee to do.

The honest forcing function is the one that would make us buyers, and it runs against us: a quarter in which new registrations fall back below 10 million and the guide gets cut. That would hand the artificial-intelligence bears their first data point, likely take the stock toward the adverse case near $215, and give us the entry the current tape refuses to offer.
valley_of_death:
There is no valley of death here in the usual sense - no cash-burn hump, no maturity wall, no solvency question. A company converting 64.5% of revenue to free cash flow, generating $1.05B on a trailing-twelve-month basis with $556M of cash, does not have a financing problem. The 2025 senior notes that matured on 2026-04-01 were refinanced cleanly and in advance with $500M of new 5.25% notes due 2032, announced in the first quarter of 2025. That is what competent treasury looks like, and it removes the classic trap.

What exists instead is a nine-month stretch where several small things all lean the same, mildly unhelpful way beneath a rising top line.

The near date is 2026-07-23, six days out - second-quarter results. The risk is asymmetric against the stock but not large: this team has raised guidance at five consecutive calls, so a raise is priced and a merely-in-line print is a small disappointment. The specific line to watch is the renewal rate, because management has now warned twice that 2026 carries a heavier mix of first-time renewals - which renew at a structurally lower rate - so the blended number can fall while nothing underneath deteriorates. The market will not parse that nuance on the day.

The 2026 guide itself is a slow drip of small negatives. Capital expenditure roughly doubles to $55-65M from $25-35M, and the reason should give any AI-adjacent holder pause: costs are "facing significantly higher costs largely attributable to intense AI industry-driven demand and supply constraints." VeriSign buys the same hardware the hyperscalers are bidding for. Operating margin is guided back down toward its long-term trend from the 2025 level. The tax rate steps to 22-25% from 21-24% on foreign taxes. Interest expense rises to $57-67M as cash balances fall and rates stay high. None of these is material alone; together they mean 2026 free cash flow roughly flatlines against 2025's $1.07B despite revenue growing about 5%.

The dated operational risk is 2026-11-01, when the .com wholesale price rises to $10.97. Management explicitly declined to promise it is free: the effect on renewals is "very dependent on what our retail registrars do pricing-wise. If they do take price increases, that could have an effect on either new registrations or renewals. And we've seen a little bit of that in the past." The registrar channel is price-unrestricted and consolidating, and it marks the wholesale price up several-fold. Any elasticity shows up in the fourth-quarter-2026 and first-quarter-2027 prints - after the increase lands, and after the catalyst window closes.

The macro overlay is mostly benign, which is itself the problem. The regime is a hawkish Federal Reserve under Chair Warsh - a hold at 3.50-3.75% with futures putting roughly 77% odds on a hike by December and rate-cut theses dead. VeriSign carries $1.24B of net debt and negative book equity, so it is not a rate beneficiary, but neither is it stressed. The one shared factor worth naming is the late-July hyperscaler earnings test of artificial-intelligence capital spending, where a guide-down would trigger broad de-grossing. VeriSign's exposure to that factor is genuinely two-sided and unusual: an AI capital-spending break would cut its hardware costs while removing the registration tailwind management now credits for part of its volume. That two-sidedness makes it a poor hedge and a poor expression of any AI view.

The real risk over the next nine months is not a drawdown. It is that nothing happens at all - the company prints two good quarters, raises guidance again, collects its price increase, and the stock does what a fairly-valued compounder does, which is track its earnings while the capital sits in it earning no excess return.
positioning_washout:
There is no washout coming, and that is precisely the problem with this setup rather than a point in its favour.

The shareholder base is about as immovable as a public register gets. Berkshire Hathaway owns close to 10% of the company - a permanent holder that has never sold, will not be forced to, and whose presence is itself widely cited as a reason to own the name. The company is its own largest buyer, returning over 100% of free cash flow: $1.13B in the twelve months to the first quarter of 2026, with $863M of buyback authorization remaining and no expiration. That is a price-insensitive bid underneath the stock every single day, shrinking the share count roughly 3.5% a year.

The question the framework asks - will a pivot or a dividend cut force yield-focused or passive holders to liquidate mechanically? - inverts here. The dividend is going the other way: initiated in the first quarter of 2025 at $0.77 and raised 5.2% to $0.81 in the fourth quarter of 2025, explicitly "consistent with the increase in net income," with management committing to "grow the dividend annually with our earnings growth." The yield is about 1.2%, which is too small to have attracted a yield-chasing base that could be flushed, but the initiation did bring in "many investors new to VeriSign" by the chief executive's own account in the second quarter of 2025 - a stickier, income-oriented cohort, not a hot one.

Smart-money and institutional flow scores read 52 and 49 out of 100 - dead neutral. No crowding to fade, no capitulation to buy. The stock sits 12% below its 52-week high and 32% above its low, 5% above its 200-day average, 60% up the 52-week range. The single sharpest recent move was a roughly 6.5% drop on 2026-04-24 - the day after a strong quarter with a price-increase announcement - and it was fully recovered within weeks. That is not a flush; that is a fairly-valued stock digesting expected news.

The only genuinely negative positioning signal is inside the building, and it is not mechanical. Open-market insider activity runs 5 buys totalling 54 shares against 51 sells totalling 37,088 shares - roughly 690-to-1 against by volume, and the honest reading of a grant-inflated buy-ratio that the screener reports as 0.00. It is routine for a mature name whose executives are paid in stock, and it should not be over-read. But it is not nothing: the people who can see the undisclosed registrar discount, the elasticity data, and the parked-domain exposure are consistent sellers into a full multiple.

The practical conclusion for a director: there is no forced seller to buy from, no dislocation to exploit, and no mechanism that would hand us a better price. The current market regime is one of violent single-name dispersion - the equal-weighted index is up 11.4% for the year against the Magnificent Seven flat, and individual names re-rate hard on events. VeriSign is the opposite of that trade: a low-beta, permanently-held, self-bidding compounder with no event. If we ever own it cheaply, it will be because something broke - a contract fight, a regulatory move on the price escalator, or the first quarter where new registrations fall and the AI-kills-the-open-web narrative finally gets a data point. Waiting for that is a real strategy. Paying $275 today is not.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now - and to be clear about why, because the reason is unusual: we are passing on a genuinely excellent company because it is priced correctly, not because anything is wrong with it.

Start with what the forensic work actually found, because it is almost entirely positive. VeriSign operates the exclusive registry for .com and .net - the internet's address book - selling wholesale to registrars at a price the US government caps, under a contract naming it sole operator through November 2030. Management guided the 2025 domain name base to roughly flat, then raised the guide at every single quarterly call and delivered +2.6%, taking the base to a record 176.1 million by the first quarter of 2026 with the 2026 guide already raised and narrowed to +3.1-4.3%. The renewal rate climbed from 72.2% to 76.3% over two years, and both the first-time and repeat legs improved - growth bought with discounts does not usually look like that. The chief executive told analysts in February exactly when the price lever would be pulled, and it was pulled on schedule in April. The credibility score is a 5 and it is earned: seven consecutive raises, all delivered, alongside voluntary disclosure of a self-inflicted headwind (a heavier first-time renewal mix in 2026 that will drag the blended rate by arithmetic). This is a wide, durable moat - a licensed monopoly layered over a genuine scale barrier, with 88.2% gross margins, a 64.5% free-cash-flow margin, and a 29-year unbroken availability record no entrant would rationally rebuild. Its trajectory is strengthening.

And none of that is a reason to buy it at $275.22.

Three independent methods converge on fair value near $272: the parts, at 22x operating profit on the core registry; a discounted cash flow at $268; and the peer-relative read, where the roughly 24x enterprise-value-to-free-cash-flow multiple sits below the quasi-monopoly toll cohort's 28-35x for the good reason that VeriSign grows 6-7% against their high-single to low-teens, and because a monopoly leased from the Department of Commerce until 2030 should not trade at an owned monopoly's multiple. When the parts, the cash flows and the comps all land within 2% of the market price, the finding is that the market has it right. Our base case offers no upside over 18 months against roughly 22% of downside to $215 on a de-rating that requires no operational break at all. There is no structural floor: no deal terms, no net cash - the company carries $1.24B of net debt against negative book equity - and a 1.2% yield is not support.

The catalyst work is decisive. The one event with real cash behind it has already fired: notice of the $0.71 increase to $10.97 was given on 2026-04-23, effective 2026-11-01, capped by contract, pre-telegraphed in February - and the shares fell about 6.5% the day after it landed alongside a strong quarter. A catalyst the market sells is a catalyst already in the price. What remains is soft: a .web arbitration running since a 2016 auction whose final hearing was set for mid-November 2025 with no outcome eight months later, and which management has quietly stopped forecasting; unquantified security services with no product, price or date; and second-quarter results on 2026-07-23 from a team whose beat is itself consensus.

The regime seals it. The current environment rewards structural special situations in thin-coverage lanes - forced sellers and spinoffs are the fattest they have been all year, with dated mechanical events on the calendar - and it punishes exactly what VeriSign is: a large-cap, permanently-held, low-beta compounder with no event, no forced seller, no activist, and nothing for an event-driven committee to do. Berkshire owns close to 10% and will not sell; the company itself bids for its own stock every day with $863M of authorization left. There is no dislocation here to exploit and no mechanism that would hand us a better price. In a dispersion regime where single names re-rate violently on events, allocating to a name with no event is the wrong trade even when the business is right.

One caution worth recording, because a careless reader would reach the opposite conclusion from the same file. The screener labels this deep value and reports a negative 26% margin of safety, a return on invested capital of negative 12,213%, a solvency score of negative 4.7, and four of five models at negative 100%. Every one of those is an artifact of negative book equity created by a decade of buybacks above book value - not evidence of distress, and not evidence of overvaluation either. A business generating $1.05B of free cash flow with $556M of cash is not insolvent. Equally, the +31% upside to a $355 target is not a street view: the consensus, median, high and low are all the same number, from one analyst at Baird, 84 days old. Both the screen's despair and the target's optimism should be discarded.

Separately from the timing call, the value case on its own merits scores a 3. Judged purely on price against our reconciled fair value and on forensic quality - ignoring the spent catalyst and the unfriendly regime - this is a high-quality franchise at an honest price with a clean file and no margin of safety. Not a trap: the base is at a record and accelerating, so the low-multiple-on-a-melting-base failure mode does not apply, and the artificial-intelligence question, while genuinely unresolved on a five-year view, currently runs the company's way on its own measured data (11.5 million new registrations in the first quarter of 2026, the most since early 2021; query volume up about 30% in nine months to 600 billion a day). But a 3 is what a fair price deserves. We do not get paid for admiring businesses.

What would change this. A quarter where new registrations fall below 10 million and the domain-base guide is cut for the first time in six quarters would hand the bears their first real data point, likely take the shares toward $215, and give us the entry this tape refuses to offer. So would a political move against the ~7% price escalator, or genuine elasticity showing up in renewals after 2026-11-01. Any of those makes VeriSign a name we want to own. Watch the 2026-07-23 print for the renewal rate specifically - and remember management has already warned that the blended number falls in 2026 for reasons that are pure arithmetic, not decay. If the market mistakes that for a crack, we should be ready to buy it.
sop_fair_value: About $272 per share (base case), against a live price of $275.22 - essentially fair value, with no margin of safety.
sop_breakdown:
Reconciling the favorable and adverse cases on the multiple, which is where they actually differ - both agree the cash flows are intact, so the argument is entirely about what a contractual monopoly with a 2030 expiry and an unresolved AI question is worth.

- .com registry: ~$1.14B of 2026 operating profit at 22x = about $25.1B. 22x is the honest midpoint: a premium to a generic mature business because the exclusivity is legally granted and the ~7% annual price escalator is contractual through 2030, but a discount to the 28-35x toll-franchise cohort (Moody's, S&P Global, MSCI, CoStar, Fair Isaac) because VeriSign grows 6-7% against their high-single to low-teens, and because their moats are not scheduled to be renegotiated with a government department.
- .net registry: ~$0.081B of operating profit at 15x = about $1.22B. Small, flat, with a real but unexercised 10% pricing right.
- Corporate and unallocated: about negative $0.6B, absorbing the doubled 2026 capital budget and the guided step-down in operating margin.
- .web: about $0.2B - roughly a 40% probability weighting on the favorable case, reflecting that a final arbitration hearing was scheduled for mid-November 2025 with no outcome reported since and that management has stopped forecasting it.
- New high-assurance security services: about $0.2B - real enough to carry a token value given management staked its closing remarks on it in two consecutive calls, too undefined to carry more.

Sum of enterprise value: about $26.1B. Less net debt of $1.24B = equity of about $24.9B on ~90.5 million shares = **about $272 per share**.

Triangulation confirms it. A discounted cash flow on $1.06B of 2026 free cash flow growing 6% for ten years, then 2.5% in perpetuity at an 8% cost of capital, yields about $268 per share. The parts and the cash flows land within 2% of each other, and within 2% of the market price of $275.22. That agreement is the finding: three independent methods say the market has this name approximately right.
risk_reward: Poor - and, unusually, poor in the specific sense that there is no reward rather than that there is unusual risk. Base-case fair value of about $272 sits fractionally below the live price of $275.22, so the central case offers no upside at all over the next 18 months beyond the roughly 1.2% dividend yield and the ~3.5% annual share-count shrink. The favorable case of $335 requires the toll-franchise cohort's multiple to be applied to a 6-7% grower and both free options (.web delegation, new security services) to pay off. The adverse case of $215 requires only a de-rating - no operational break, no lost contract, no earnings miss - and lands about 22% below today. So the market is offering roughly 22% of downside for roughly 22% of upside, with the base case at zero. There is no structural floor beneath the price: no deal terms, no net cash (the company carries $1.24B of net debt), no tender. The 52-week low of $208.86 is a chart level, not support.
peer_comps_note:
The peer file supplies no live peer override or anchor multiple, so the multiples here are reasoned from the peer set with an explicit growth adjustment rather than borrowed from memory. The peer read is that VeriSign has almost no true public comparable: GoDaddy is the closest same-industry name but is a registrar - a reseller with structurally lower margins - not a toll-collecting registry, making it a weak comp. The better economic match is the quasi-monopoly subscription-toll cohort (Moody's, S&P Global, MSCI, CoStar, Fair Isaac), which trades around 28-35x free cash flow on 40-55% net margins and similar pricing power. VeriSign at about 24x enterprise value to free cash flow screens modestly cheap to that cohort and rich to GoDaddy.

The discount is explained, not free. The peer file's own verdict is "in line," and its reasoning holds up: VeriSign grows revenue 6.4% and earnings per share about 10% against a cohort compounding high-single to low-teens, and the gap in growth accounts for the gap in multiple rather than flagging a mispricing. Two adjustments are needed on top. First, a genuine discount is warranted that the cohort does not carry: VeriSign's exclusivity is a contract with a November 2030 expiry and a government-set price cap, while Moody's and MSCI own their franchises outright and set their own prices - a licensed monopoly should not trade at an owned monopoly's multiple. That is why the base case anchors the core registry at 22x operating profit rather than the cohort's high-20s. Second, the four valuation models reading a negative 100% margin of safety must be discarded, not weighed: they are artifacts of negative book equity created by a decade of buybacks above book value, not evidence of overvaluation, and the same artifact drives the reported return on invested capital to negative 12,213% and the solvency score to negative 4.7. The Graham-revised method, the only one that handles this balance sheet cleanly, reads about +8%. Three independent approaches - parts at 22x, a discounted cash flow at $268, and the peer-relative read - converge on fair value near today's price. This is not sector-beta compression masquerading as alpha; it is simply a fairly-priced franchise.
interrogator_dossier:
# VeriSign (VRSN) — A Deep Dive on Management and the Setup
*Forensic dossier · five consecutive quarterly calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) tested against the financials · prepared 2026-07-17 · share price used: $275.22 (Nasdaq, US dollars)*

---

## 1. Narrative Arc

**The takeaway: this is the rare case where a management team promised a turn, described the exact mechanism, and then delivered it four quarters running — and the story got *bigger*, not smaller, as it went.**

VeriSign operates the exclusive registry for .com and .net domain names. It does not sell to the public; it sells wholesale to accredited registrars (GoDaddy and hundreds of others) at a price the US government caps. Think of it as a toll booth on the internet's address book, with the toll rate set by contract.

The arc across these five calls moves through three distinct phases.

**Phase one — apologetic recovery (Q1 2025).** The company opened 2025 guiding the domain name base to somewhere between *shrinking* 0.7% and *growing* 0.9% — a genuinely defensive number. The language was hedged: management said the guide "includes a measure of caution until the macroeconomic situation clarifies," and CEO Jim Bidzos volunteered "I'm not an economist, but I think I can recognize a bit of turmoil here." The stated recovery mechanism was two-part and specific: (a) new marketing programs rolled out to registrars in late 2024, and (b) a hoped-for cyclical shift in registrar behavior from squeezing revenue per customer back toward acquiring new customers. Bidzos flagged two registrars buying Super Bowl ads as his evidence the shift was starting.

**Phase two — vindication and escalation (Q2–Q4 2025).** The domain guide was raised at *every single call*: to +1.2%/+2.0% in Q2, to +2.2%/+2.5% in Q3, and the year actually closed at **+2.6% (4.5 million names added)** — above the top of the guide it had set only three months earlier and roughly 2.5 percentage points above where the year started. Renewal rates, the single most important quality metric in this business, climbed from 72.7% (Q2 2024) to 75.5% (Q2 2025) to 75.3% in Q3 against 72.2% a year prior. The hedging language disappeared.

**Phase three — offense (Q4 2025 → Q1 2026).** Two genuinely new growth drivers were *introduced*, not dropped:
1. **New services.** In Q4 2025 Bidzos previewed that "we now believe we have strong candidates for new services that can help reduce known and unknown vulnerabilities and contribute significantly to information trust." By Q1 2026 this had firmed into a promised blog series on "high assurance infrastructure" starting "as soon as next month." This is the first time in years the company has signalled it would *add* a business rather than divest one.
2. **The price lever re-armed.** On the Q4 2025 call (Feb 2026) Bidzos told analysts the first allowable .com price increase "will come to execute in October 2026" and that an announcement, if made, would land in April. It landed in April — see section 4.

Meanwhile the artificial-intelligence question migrated from a defensive answer to an offensive one. In Q2 2025 Bidzos answered an AI question with "We don't see it as a negative" — a denial. By Q1 2026 the framing was affirmative and specific: "we see a positive impact from AI tools, which make content and website creation faster and easier," backed by 11.5 million new registrations, the most since the first half of 2021.

**One driver quietly de-emphasized:** .web. It received a substantive update in Q1 2025 and Q2 2025 ("final hearing... mid-November 2025"), a "nothing substantive that's new" in Q3 2025, and by Q1 2026 the conversation had shifted entirely to ICANN's *new* top-level-domain round opening in April 2026. A driver that quietly stops being discussed is a driver management has stopped underwriting.

---

## 2. Claims vs Financials (forensic)

Management's biggest claims tested against the actual trajectory:

| Claim (quarter) | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Improving trends... registrars shifting towards customer acquisition" (Q1 2025) | Domain base: 169.8M (Q1 2025) → 170.5M → 171.9M → 173.5M → **176.1M (Q1 2026)**. New registrations 10.1M → 10.4M → 10.6M → 10.7M → **11.5M**. Renewal rate 75.3% → 75.5% → 75.3% → 75.0% → **76.3%** | **Confirmed, and then some.** Both the volume and the quality legs improved together — the hard part |
| Revenue growth is durable | 2021 $1.33B → 2025 $1.66B (+6.4% in 2025, 3-year compound rate +5.2%); Q1 2026 $429M, +6.6% | **Confirmed but modest.** This is a 6–7% grower. The narrative's energy exceeds the top line's | 
| "Sound financial discipline" / margin stability | Gross margin 88.2% and stable; net margin 49.8%; free cash flow margin 64.5%. Operating income $1.12B on $1.66B revenue in 2025 (67.5%) | **Confirmed.** Among the most profitable businesses in public markets |
| "Returned over 100% of our free cash flow" (Q1 2026) | $1.13B returned over twelve months against trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of $1.05B. 2025: $1.1B returned. Buyback authorization $863M remaining at Q1 2026 | **Confirmed — and it is funded partly by the balance sheet, not just earnings** (see below) |
| Earnings per share growth | $7.00 (2021) → $6.24 (2022) → $7.90 → $8.00 → **$8.81 (2025)**, +10.1%; trailing-twelve-month $9.05; Q1 2026 $2.34, +11.4% | **Confirmed.** Note the five-year compound rate is only +5.9% — the 2022 dip drags it. Recent-year growth is genuinely ~10% |

**Where the story is richer than the trajectory justifies — and where the numbers mislead:**

*The screener's returns figures are meaningless here and must not be used.* Return on equity of −47.1% and return on invested capital of −12,213% are not signs of a broken business; they are arithmetic artifacts of **negative book equity** created by a decade of buying back stock above book value. The same artifact drives the Altman-Z solvency score to −4.7 and forces four of five valuation models (discounted cash flow, earnings power value, owner earnings, and the deep-value model) to read −100% margin of safety. A company generating $1.05B of free cash flow on $1.66B of revenue with $556M of cash is not insolvent. The only model that handles this balance sheet cleanly, the Graham-revised method, reads roughly +8%. **Any director reading the returns line as evidence of decay is reading an accounting shadow.**

*The real gap between narrative and numbers is growth arithmetic.* EPS grows ~10% while revenue grows ~6.5%. The wedge is the buyback — roughly 3.5% annual share-count shrink. That is real value creation, but it means about a third of the earnings growth is financial engineering funded increasingly by debt: net debt is **$1.24 billion** as of 2026-03-31 (borrowings $1.79B plus $6M capitalized leases, less $556M cash; the figure excluding leases is ~$1.23B). Cash has drifted down across the five calls — $649M → $594M → $618M → $581M → **$556M** — while debt stayed. Returning more than 100% of free cash flow is a choice that cannot compound forever without leverage rising.

*One genuine cost inflection is buried in the Q4 2025 guide.* Capital expenditure for 2026 is guided to **$55–65M against $25–35M in 2025** — roughly a doubling. The stated reason is candid and important: end-of-life equipment replacement and capacity expansion "facing significantly higher costs largely attributable to intense AI industry-driven demand and supply constraints." VeriSign is a *buyer* of the same hardware the AI build-out is bidding up. Management also guided 2026 operating margin back to "our long-term trend as compared with the level we saw during 2025" — a polite way of saying margin steps *down* modestly this year. The screener flags margins at 1.08 standard deviations above their historical peak; management is telling you the same thing in words.

---

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Rating: Rising, decisively — and it rose in step with the evidence rather than ahead of it.**

- **Q1 2025 — hedged, defensive.** "Includes a measure of caution until the macroeconomic situation clarifies." Bidzos on the macro: "It's a question of clarity... a bit of uncertainty about where things will land." On the marketing programs: "it's still early... we still have some work to do." This is a management team refusing to bank a recovery it could see but not yet prove.
- **Q2 2025 — confidence with a governor.** "Our updated guidance reflects this positive momentum but continues to reflect some conservatism as economic and geopolitical uncertainty exists." Note the construction: momentum is now asserted; conservatism is now a choice rather than a fear. On 2026 programs: "I can tell you with confidence that what we're learning is giving us cause for a reason to believe that we think we can improve them."
- **Q3 2025 — plain-spoken and unhedged.** "We're seeing solid underlying demand." The macro caveat is gone entirely. New: "we also see increases in registration and resolution activity for which we believe increasing use of AI is... a primary driver" — management now claiming AI as a tailwind on the record.
- **Q4 2025 — expansionary.** "2025 marked another solid year." Then the pivot to offense: "we now believe we have strong candidates for new services."
- **Q1 2026 — the most confident of the five.** "VeriSign delivered strong results... both operationally and financially." Not "sequentially improving trends" (the Q1/Q2 2025 formulation) — *strong*. Guidance was **raised and narrowed simultaneously** (1.5–3.5% → 3.1–4.3%), which is the specific move of a team that believes its own forecast.

**The offense/defense test:** the language moved unambiguously from defensive (macro, caution, clarity, cost discipline) to offensive (record base, new services, price increase, capacity expansion). Guidance also became *more* specific over time, not less — the domain-base range narrowed from a 1.6-point spread to a 1.2-point spread. Teams hiding something widen their ranges.

**One honest note on precision:** when pressed by JPMorgan's Alexei Gogolev in Q4 2025 on whether the guide implied a second-half taper, CFO John Calys answered "I feel like I'd be splitting hairs to explain that one-tenth of a percent," then *did* explain the actual mechanic — a heavier mix of first-time renewals in 2026 that mathematically drags the blended renewal rate. That is a real, self-inflicted headwind disclosed voluntarily and repeatedly. It is the opposite of promotion.

---

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**Score: High.** This is the strongest section of the file.

| Guide given | Where it was set | Where it landed | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025 domain base growth | Q1 2025: −0.7% to +0.9% | **+2.6% actual** | Beat the *top* of the original range by 1.7 points |
| — raised Q2 2025 | +1.2% to +2.0% | +2.6% | Beat again |
| — raised Q3 2025 | +2.2% to +2.5% | +2.6% | Beat again |
| 2025 revenue | Q1 2025: $1.635–1.650B | **$1.66B** | Beat the top |
| — raised Q2 2025 | $1.645–1.655B | $1.66B | Beat the top |
| — raised Q3 2025 | $1.652–1.657B | $1.66B | Delivered at the top |
| 2026 domain base | Q4 2025: 1.5–3.5% | Q1 2026: **raised and narrowed to 3.1–4.3%** | Tracking above |
| 2026 revenue | Q4 2025: $1.715–1.735B | Q1 2026: **raised to $1.730–1.745B** | Tracking above |
| .com price increase | Q4 2025 (Feb): "first opportunity... would be an announcement made in April" | **Announced 2026-04-23**: +$0.71 to $10.97, effective 2026-11-01 | Delivered on the exact predicted timeline |

Reconciled against the screener's earnings-beat rate of 5 of 7 quarters (71%), the picture is coherent: this team guides low and delivers high, and the pattern held across seven consecutive raises. **There is a sandbagging pattern, and it is systematic rather than occasional** — the 2025 opening guide of "roughly flat" against a delivered +2.6% is not a forecasting error, it is a posture. A director should treat the 2026 guide of 3.1–4.3% as a floor rather than a midpoint, but should equally note that a *known* sandbagger's beats carry less surprise value: the market has now watched this movie five times and prices the beat.

The one blemish is the Q4 2025 tax line: net income fell sequentially ($213M → $206M) on "higher income tax expense... primarily due to foreign-based income taxes," and the 2026 tax-rate guide stepped up to 22–25% from 21–24%. Small, disclosed, unspun.

---

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

**What analysts keep pushing on:**

1. **Marketing programs — what exactly are they?** Asked in all five calls (Baird's Rob Oliver and Citi's Ygal Arounian repeatedly). Management's answers are consistently *directional* rather than quantified: "good registrar interest," "early adopters," "an evolution than a revolution." The one hard disclosure came in Q3 2025 when Calys admitted the programs "are accounted for as a reduction in revenue" — meaning the cost is netted against the top line and is therefore **invisible to investors as a discrete number**. When Arounian pressed directly on "has there been a lot of discounting within that?", the answer was a non-answer: the programs "yield higher quality and higher renewing names." **This is the single least transparent area of the story.** Reported revenue growth of 6.4% is *after* an undisclosed discount, and only management knows the gross figure.
2. **Pricing.** Deflected by stated policy in every call ("we don't guide to pricing"). This deflection turned out to be honest rather than evasive — the increase arrived exactly when Bidzos said the window would open.
3. **AI and the open web.** Pushed hard from Q2 2025 onward. Management's answers evolved from philosophical to data-backed, which is the right direction, but the deepest version of the bear question — *do autonomous AI agents need human-readable domain names at all?* — has never been answered with data, only with assertion ("we believe demand for persistent, resolvable identities and endpoints will continue").
4. **Price elasticity after the increase.** Citi's Jamesmichael Sherman-Lewis asked in Q1 2026 what the Nov-1 increase does to renewals. Calys's answer was properly humble: "it's very dependent on what our retail registrars do pricing-wise. If they do take price increases, that could have an effect on either new registrations or renewals. And we've seen a little bit of that in the past." **Management is explicitly not promising the price increase is free.** Bidzos softened it with "about $0.03 a day" — a rhetorical minimisation of a wholesale price that registrars mark up several-fold.
5. **A topic analysts pushed on that became bad news:** expenses. Oliver asked in Q1 2025 whether the higher expense run-rate was permanent. It was — operating expense went $131M → $129M → $135M → $140M → $135M, and 2026 brought a doubled capital budget on top.

**What analysts are *not* asking that they should be:** nobody has pressed on the negative book equity, the $1.24B net debt, or the sustainability of returning more than 100% of free cash flow while cash declines. Nobody has asked what happens at the .com contract's 2030 expiry.

---

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🟢 **Green — the guidance record.** Seven consecutive raises across 2025 and into 2026, each delivered. (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026.)

🟢 **Green — the quality leg improved with the volume leg.** Renewal rate 72.2% (Q3 2024) → 76.3% (Q1 2026). Growth bought with discounts usually shows up as volume without retention. This did the opposite, and Calys disclosed in Q3 2025 that *both* first-time and previously-renewing rates improved — the harder, more honest cut of the number.

🟢 **Green — the price lever fired exactly as forecast** and is contractually secured: +$0.71 to $10.97 effective 2026-11-01 (announced 2026-04-23), the first of four allowable ~7% annual increases in the back half of the six-year term that began October 2024 under the .com registry agreement running to 2030.

🟢 **Green — capital returns are real and consistent.** $1.1B in 2025, $1.13B in the twelve months to Q1 2026, buyback authorization raised by $913M in Q2 2025, dividend initiated Q1 2025 at $0.77 and raised 5.2% to $0.81 in Q4 2025 "consistent with the increase in net income."

🟢 **Green — management transition executed cleanly.** CFO George Kilguss retired May 2025 after thirteen years; John Calys, the prior controller and a former interim CFO, stepped in with no guidance discontinuity and, if anything, more numerical candour (the renewal-mix disclosure was his).

🔴 **Red — the growth is being purchased with an undisclosed discount that is netted against revenue** (Q3 2025 admission). Investors cannot see the gross price, the discount, or the incremental cost per name. This is the one place where the reported numbers could be flattering the story and no outside party can check.

🔴 **Red — insider behaviour contradicts the narrative.** Open-market activity is **5 buys totalling 54 shares against 51 sells totalling 37,088 shares**. The people telling you the story are net sellers by a factor of roughly 690-to-1 by volume. (The screener's buy-ratio of 0.00 and the "bull score 6" should be read through this, not around it.)

🔴 **Red — margin and cost inflection acknowledged for 2026.** Capital expenditure roughly doubling to $55–65M on AI-driven hardware inflation; operating margin guided back toward "long-term trend"; tax rate stepping to 22–25%; interest expense rising to $57–67M. Every line of the 2026 guide points slightly the wrong way beneath a rising top line.

🔴 **Red — .web has gone quiet.** Five calls, four updates, decreasing substance: a "final hearing" scheduled for mid-November 2025 has produced no reported outcome as of today. A ten-year dispute that management describes as "abuse of process... pursued in bad faith" is a driver they cannot control and have stopped forecasting.

🔴 **Amber — cash is drifting down** ($649M → $556M across five quarters) while more than 100% of free cash flow is returned and net debt sits at $1.24B. Not remotely a solvency issue at these cash flows; it is a limit on how long the buyback can keep out-running earnings.

---

## 7. Hidden Signals

**The most important terminology shift in the file is "high assurance."** It appears nowhere in Q1 2025. By Q1 2026 Bidzos spends a full closing section defining it — 100% availability for 29 years, cryptographically protected answers, sub-millisecond response across 600 billion daily queries (up from "over 460 billion" quoted in Q2 2025, a ~30% rise in nine months), "multiple orders of magnitude" excess capacity. **This is a company building the vocabulary for a product it has not yet announced.** Read alongside the Q4 2025 line about "strong candidates for new services... offered to new or existing customers throughout our channel," it says management intends to sell security services on top of the registry. That would be the first business expansion after years of divestitures — genuinely new, entirely unquantified, and not in any model.

**The AI framing inverted, and the honest version is more nuanced than either side's slogan.** Bidzos's Q1 2026 mention that "with Anthropic's Mythos, we've seen that AI is capable of revealing vulnerabilities in various systems" is the tell: he is positioning AI-discovered vulnerability as the *demand driver* for the new security services. So AI is simultaneously (a) a volume tailwind today via easier website creation, (b) a cost headwind via hardware inflation, (c) the justification for a new product line, and (d) the existential question about whether the open web survives agentic browsing. Management addresses (a), (b) and (c) with data and dodges (d) with conviction.

**A quiet admission about a neighbouring business.** Asked about Google's AdSense change hurting parked-domain monetisation, Bidzos said of that model: "yes, you've been on a downhill slide for 15 years" — and then declined to size his own exposure: "I don't have a segment breakout in detail. We do some analysis, but we don't disclose that." He is telling you a slice of the domain base exists for advertising monetisation that has been structurally dying since Google's Panda update in 2011, and that he will not tell you how big it is.

**On competition, the posture is a legal one, not a commercial one.** VeriSign never discusses competing on product or price against other top-level domains — because it cannot; it is "prohibited from selling .com registrations to retail buyers" and "may only sell to accredited registrars and only at a capped regulated price" (Q1 2026). Its competitive discussion is entirely about ICANN process and arbitration. That is what a regulated monopoly sounds like: the risk isn't a competitor, it's the contract.

**On the channel, an under-appreciated dependency.** Bidzos volunteers that the channel is consolidating — "Some have been acquired, some have merged" — and Gogolev's Q1 2026 question named GoDaddy "your biggest customer." A registry with a capped price selling through a consolidating, price-unrestricted channel has a long-term bargaining problem that no call has addressed.

---

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

Every operating metric that matters is better than it was five quarters ago, and the improvement was *predicted by management before it happened*: the domain base is at a record 176.1 million and accelerating (2025 guide started at roughly flat and delivered +2.6%; 2026 guide already raised to +3.1–4.3%), the renewal rate has climbed roughly four points in two years, revenue growth accelerated from 4.7% to 6.6%, and the pricing lever — dormant for two years — is re-armed with three more ~7% increases available through the contract's 2030 expiry.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: none of this is a secret, and the price already reflects it.** At $275.22 the shares trade at roughly 30 times trailing earnings and about 24 times enterprise value to free cash flow, roughly 12% below the 52-week high of $312.48 and 32% above the low. The re-rate on the two things a newcomer would call catalysts — the recovery in domain growth and the price increase — has already occurred. The stock actually *fell about 6.5% the day after* the strong Q1 2026 report that contained the price-increase announcement (2026-04-24), which is the market's way of saying it was expecting exactly that. There is no dislocation to buy, no forced seller, no activist, and no argument the market has missed. **The director is not being asked to buy a mispricing; he is being asked to pay a fair price for a very good business — and to decide whether that is what this book is for.** The forensic file is clean; the entry is not cheap.

**Economic moat: WIDE. Moat type: regulatory-license, layered over scale-cost.**

The evidence supports the width without needing the accounting returns (which are unusable — negative book equity from buybacks makes return on invested capital arithmetically meaningless here, not economically bad). Judge it on margins and durability instead: gross margin 88.2% and stable, operating margin ~68%, free cash flow margin 64.5%, and — the real proof — a contract that names VeriSign the sole registry for .com through November 2030 with a legally guaranteed right to raise prices ~7% in each of four years, plus a renewal presumption that has been exercised repeatedly since 1997. The switching cost is absolute at the registrant level: a business does not change its .com address. The 29-year unbroken availability record and "multiple orders of magnitude" of excess capacity are a real, expensive, scale-funded barrier that no new entrant would rationally rebuild.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Not widening — management itself guides 2026 operating margin *down* toward the long-term trend, capital intensity is roughly doubling on AI-driven hardware inflation, and the price cap is regulated rather than earned. Not eroding either — volumes, renewals and the price lever all moved favourably. Stable is the honest read.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE — and this is a live debate, not a settled one.**

The structural bear case is the generative-AI displacement of the open web: if users ask an assistant rather than typing an address, and if AI agents transact through machine identifiers rather than human-readable names, the demand for a memorable .com decays and the long tail of the domain base — including the advertising-monetised parked slice Bidzos concedes has been "on a downhill slide for 15 years" — shrinks. That would impair terminal value, not just a year's growth.

Three things keep this at manageable rather than material today. First, the measured data currently runs the *other* way: 11.5 million new registrations in Q1 2026 is the highest since early 2021, and query volume rose ~30% in nine months to 600 billion per day — reliance on the resolution layer is *rising* with AI, not falling. Second, the revenue model is a per-name annual toll with a contractual price escalator, so a slow-decaying base can be offset by price for years. Third, even the aggressive bear case is a decade-long diffusion, and VeriSign holds a contract to 2030 with ~7% annual pricing through it.

**Therefore the cheapness question resolves cleanly: this is neither a fear-print nor a value trap — because it isn't cheap.** The base is not structurally shrinking (it is at a record and accelerating), so the value-trap label is wrong on the facts. But there is no mispricing to harvest either: the shares sit at a fair-to-full multiple against a quasi-monopoly cohort, and the discount to that cohort is explained by VeriSign's slower growth rather than by market error. A director should size this as a quality holding at a fair price if that is the mandate — and should not pretend it is a special situation.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 5 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: WIDE | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable
